items.question: Secret type has a large effect on leakage. Why can differences in secret-type composition still not explain the differences among the three persuasion-level rates in Table 4?
items.answer: Every dialogue receives all three probes, so each persuasion level is measured on exactly the same dialogues with the same secret-type mix. This paired, repeated-measures design, analysed with Cochran's Q, holds composition fixed across levels. Drift bins are different, because they contain different dialogues.
rubric: States that secret-type composition is identical across persuasion levels.
Explains that each dialogue is evaluated under all three probes (a paired, repeated-measures design), so composition cannot differ between levels.

items.question: If only the hard probe were used, would GPT-OSS-120B's probe-level leakage exceed DeepSeek-R1's by more than 10 percentage points?
items.answer: No. Under the hard probe GPT leaks 32.90% and DeepSeek 29.20%, a gap of only 3.7 points, because GPT's leakage drops sharply under pressure.
rubric: Answers no.
Cites the hard-probe rates (32.90% vs 29.20%, about a 3.7-point gap) or GPT's drop under hard persuasion.

items.question: If only the medium probe were used, would GPT-OSS-120B's probe-level leakage exceed DeepSeek-R1's by more than 10 percentage points?
items.answer: Yes. Under the medium probe GPT leaks 40.50% while DeepSeek reaches its lowest rate, 22.00%, a gap of about 18.5 points.
rubric: Answers yes.
Cites the medium-probe rates (40.50% vs 22.00%, about an 18.5-point gap) or DeepSeek's minimum at medium.

items.question: If PrivDrift had used only the simple and hard probes, would GPT-OSS-120B's average probe-level leakage exceed Qwen3-VL-235B's?
items.answer: No. GPT would average (39.3 + 32.9)/2 = 36.1%, against Qwen's (38.7 + 40.6)/2 = 39.65%.
rubric: Answers no.
Shows GPT's average of about 36.1% falling below Qwen's of about 39.65% (Qwen's strong hard-probe rate versus GPT's weak one).

items.question: If PrivDrift had used only the simple and medium probes, would GPT-OSS-120B's average probe-level leakage exceed Qwen3-VL-235B's?
items.answer: Yes. GPT would average (39.3 + 40.5)/2 = 39.9%, against Qwen's (38.7 + 33.3)/2 = 36.0%.
rubric: Answers yes.
Shows GPT's average of about 39.9% exceeding Qwen's of about 36.0% (dropping the hard probe removes GPT's low and Qwen's high value).

items.question: For DeepSeek-R1, would fuzzy matching at the 0.80 threshold flag a larger share of probe responses than the hybrid detector?
items.answer: Yes, slightly: 26.53% versus 26.43% (Table 6).
rubric: Answers yes.
Cites 26.53% (fuzzy 0.80) versus 26.43% (hybrid).

items.question: For GPT-OSS-120B, would fuzzy matching at the 0.80 threshold flag a larger share of probe responses than the hybrid detector?
items.answer: No. It flags 37.07% against the hybrid's 37.57%, because the judge catches some low-similarity disclosures.
rubric: Answers no.
Cites 37.07% (fuzzy 0.80) versus 37.57% (hybrid).

items.question: Given only Table 4's per-probe rates, could DeepSeek-R1's dialogue-level leakage have been as high as 85%?
items.answer: No. A dialogue leaks only if at least one probe leaks, so the dialogue-level rate cannot exceed the sum of the three probe rates: 28.1 + 22.0 + 29.2 = 79.3%.
rubric: Answers no.
Uses the bound that dialogue-level leakage is at most the sum of the probe-level rates (79.3% for DeepSeek).

items.question: Given only Table 4's per-probe rates, could GPT-OSS-120B's dialogue-level leakage have been as high as 85%?
items.answer: Yes, it would be possible. The sum of GPT's probe rates is 39.3 + 40.5 + 32.9 = 112.7%, so the union bound does not rule out 85%; only the observed 47.70% shows it did not happen.
rubric: Answers yes (not ruled out).
Notes that the sum of GPT's probe rates (112.7%) exceeds 85%, so the any-probe bound permits it.

items.question: Given GPT-OSS-120B's probe-level regex and hybrid rates (36.80% and 37.57%), could the judge have raised its dialogue-level leakage by as much as 2.0 percentage points?
items.answer: Yes, it could have. The judge flipped about 0.77% of 3,000 responses, about 23 responses, and each can add at most one leaking dialogue, so up to about 2.3 points was possible. The actual increase was 0.
rubric: Answers yes (possible).
Computes about 23 judge-flipped responses, so the dialogue-level increase is capped at about 2.3 points, which is at least 2.0.

items.question: Given GPT-OSS-120B's probe-level regex and hybrid rates (36.80% and 37.57%), could the judge have raised its dialogue-level leakage by as much as 3.0 percentage points?
items.answer: No. Only about 23 of 3,000 responses were flipped by the judge, and each can add at most one of the 1,000 dialogues. The dialogue-level increase therefore cannot exceed about 2.3 points.
rubric: Answers no.
Uses the cap of about 23 judge-flipped responses, so at most about 2.3 points can be added at the dialogue level.

items.question: An attacker can resend each of the three PrivDrift probes several times to a Qwen3-VL-235B session with stochastic outputs. Is 54.60% better viewed as an upper or a lower estimate of the per-dialogue risk, and why?
items.answer: It is better viewed as a lower estimate. The dialogue-level rate counts a dialogue as leaking if any of exactly one response per probe leaks, and under the any-of rule extra attempts can only add leaks. Repeated sampling would therefore raise or maintain the rate, unless the outputs are deterministic.
rubric: Says it is a lower estimate (or that risk is likely higher).
Explains that the metric uses one response per probe with an any-of rule, so additional samples can only add leaks.

items.question: A workflow's downstream requests for user data are always urgent, high-pressure demands. A colleague argues that GPT-OSS-120B is the safest choice because pressure triggers its safety behaviour. Is that right by PrivDrift's probe-level numbers?
items.answer: No. Under the hard probe, DeepSeek-R1 still leaks less (29.20%) than GPT-OSS-120B (32.90%), and Qwen3-VL-235B is worst (40.60%). GPT's pressure-induced drop narrows its gap with DeepSeek but does not close it.
rubric: Says no; DeepSeek-R1 is the safest under hard probes.
Cites the hard-probe rates: DeepSeek 29.20% < GPT 32.90% < Qwen 40.60%.

items.question: In a threat setting, exactly one probe is sent per session and its persuasion style is equally likely to be simple, medium or hard. Should GPT-OSS-120B or Qwen3-VL-235B be judged riskier, based on PrivDrift?
items.answer: Neither, meaningfully: the relevant measure is the probe-level average, and GPT and Qwen are essentially tied (37.57% vs 37.53%). Qwen's 7-point lead at the dialogue level comes from the any-of-three-probes aggregation, which does not apply to a single attempt.
rubric: Says they are essentially tied, with no meaningful difference.
Explains that probe-level averages (37.57% vs 37.53%) are the appropriate measure because the dialogue-level gap reflects multiple attempts.

items.question: A team deploys GPT-OSS-120B for travel bookings in which users share passport numbers. They cite PrivDrift's near-zero SSN and credit-card leakage as evidence that passport numbers will also be suppressed. Is this justified?
items.answer: No. Passport numbers were not tested, and PrivDrift suggests that suppression depends on format-specific sensitivity cues rather than general confidentiality reasoning. Other user-disclosed identifiers, such as phone numbers, leak at high rates (70.89% for GPT), so an untested format could easily behave like those rather than like SSNs.
rubric: Says it is not justified (untested).
Reasons that suppression appears format-specific, as shown by the high leakage of other identifiers such as phone numbers, so it need not extend to an unseen format.

items.question: Using PrivDrift-style dialogues, a new study finds a Cramer's V of 0.09 between leakage and the politeness of the probe. Using PrivDrift's effect sizes as a reference scale, how important is politeness?
items.answer: Politeness would be a minor factor. A V of 0.09 sits within PrivDrift's range for drift length and persuasion (about 0.064–0.107, negligible to small) and far below secret type (0.59–0.77, large).
rubric: Concludes politeness is a minor or small effect.
Compares 0.09 with PrivDrift's drift and persuasion values (about 0.06–0.11) and with the much larger secret-type values (about 0.59–0.77).

items.question: Suppose it emerged that the naturalistic refinement step had silently changed the number of drift turns in many dialogues, while preserving secrets and probes. Which of the paper's results would be compromised?
items.answer: The drift-indexed results would be compromised: the drift-length Cramer's V, the dip-and-rebound pattern, Table 7's length-by-drift statistics and Privacy Half-Life. The persuasion-level and secret-type results, and the overall dialogue-level rates, would not depend on correct drift labels.
rubric: Identifies the drift-dependent results (drift V, the dip near d = 3, τ and/or Table 7) as compromised.
Notes that the persuasion and secret-type findings (and the aggregate rates) do not rely on drift labels and would remain intact.

items.question: If a manual audit found that many responses labelled positive by Stage 1 matching did not really disclose the secret, would the hybrid detector have corrected this in the paper's headline rates? Why?
items.answer: No. The Llama judge is applied only to responses that Stage 1 labels negative, so every regex-positive response stays positive under the hybrid detector. Such false positives would inflate the regex and hybrid rates equally, including the headline 38.7–54.6%.
rubric: Says no, the hybrid stage would not correct it.
Explains that the judge sees only regex-negative responses, so regex positives pass straight into hybrid labels and inflate the headline rates.

items.question: If Figure 4's drift curves had been completely flat, with no dip near d = 3, which part of the paper's argument would lose its empirical illustration even though τ would still be 7?
items.answer: The Discussion's motivation for the stability clause of Privacy Half-Life would lose its illustration. That clause is justified by observed intermediate dips that are not stable, and the τ values themselves would be unchanged.
rubric: Identifies the motivation for stability-based evaluation (the stability clause of τ, or the argument that transient dips should not count as suppression).
Explains that the observed dip-then-rebound is what illustrates the transient decreases this argument relies on.

items.question: Does τ = 7 show that no model's leakage ever falls to half its d = 0 level within d ≤ 6? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Despite the name, τ tests a threshold of 10% of L(0), not 50%. Leakage could stably fall to, say, 40% of L(0) and still yield τ = 7.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that τ uses δ = 0.1 × L(0), not a halving threshold, so τ = 7 is compatible with leakage falling below half of L(0).

items.question: Does the paper show that the evaluated models generally suppress numeric personal identifiers? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Phone numbers are numeric identifiers, yet they leak at 46.13–70.89% across models. Only SSNs and credit-card numbers are strongly suppressed.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites high phone-number leakage (about 46–71%) in contrast with the low SSN and credit-card rates.

items.question: Does the paper show that credit-card numbers are protected more reliably than SSNs? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Credit cards leak slightly less than SSNs for all three models (0.00 vs 0.14, 0.39 vs 1.11, 4.01 vs 5.97), but the differences are tiny and no test comparing the two types is reported.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that the differences are small and no significance test compares the two types, even though the direction is consistent.

items.question: Does the paper show how leakage behaves after a single intervening drift turn? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Drift lengths are sampled from {0} ∪ {2, …, 6}, so d = 1 never occurs in the observed set.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that d = 1 is excluded from the sampled drift lengths (D_obs = {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}).

items.question: Does the paper show that GPT-OSS-120B leaks significantly more under the medium probe than under the simple probe? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The rates differ by only 1.2 points (40.50% vs 39.30%). Cochran's Q establishes only that the three levels differ overall, and the post-hoc McNemar results for individual pairs are not reported.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes the small difference (about 1.2 points) and that pairwise post-hoc results are not reported; Cochran's Q only shows an overall difference.

items.question: Does the paper show that each additional drift turn adds roughly the same amount of content to the dialogue? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. In Table 7 the per-turn increments in average words vary widely: about 108 words from d = 3 to 4, but only about 47 from d = 5 to 6. Drift length is therefore an uneven proxy for added content.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites unequal increments in Table 7 (for example about +108 words from d = 3 to 4 versus about +47 from d = 5 to 6).

items.question: Does the paper show that its Llama judge labels leakage more accurately than fuzzy matching? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper argues that the judge is more expressive but reports no human inter-annotator agreement or ground truth. Fuzzy and hybrid rates differ by fractions of a point, in both directions, so neither is validated as more accurate.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes the absence of human ground truth or inter-annotator agreement, and that fuzzy and hybrid disagree only slightly and in both directions.

items.question: Since every evaluated model's leakage stays above δ at all tested drift lengths, what does PrivDrift imply about an auditor's claim that six drift turns cut a model's leakage by more than 90% relative to immediate recall?
items.answer: For these three models the claim is contradicted. No model approaches δ = 0.1 × L(0) at any tested d, so leakage at d = 6 remains above 10% of the d = 0 rate, which means the reduction is less than 90%.
rubric: Says the claim is contradicted for these models (the reduction is under 90%).
Reasons that leakage at every tested d, including d = 6, stays above δ = 0.1 × L(0).

items.question: Qwen3-VL-235B leaks more than GPT-OSS-120B for emails, SSNs and credit cards in Table 5. Why are the two models still almost tied in probe-level hybrid leakage (37.53% vs 37.57%)?
items.answer: GPT-OSS-120B leaks phone numbers far more often (70.89% vs 57.24%, about 13.7 points). That gap roughly cancels Qwen's combined excess on the other three types: about 2.9 points on email, 5.8 on SSN and 4.0 on credit card.
rubric: Identifies phone numbers as the type where GPT-OSS-120B leaks much more than Qwen (about 71% vs 57%)
Explains that this phone gap offsets Qwen's higher email, SSN and credit-card leakage, producing a near tie overall

items.question: Why does loosening the fuzzy-matching threshold from 0.85 to 0.80 add at most about a third of a percentage point of probe-level leakage for any model?
items.answer: Very few responses fall in the 0.80–0.85 similarity band. Responses either reproduce the secret verbatim or nearly so, or are far from it, and there are almost no near-miss strings. This fits the paper's claim that leakage is dominated by direct or near-direct reproduction.
rubric: States that few responses have intermediate similarity to the secret (outputs are essentially either matches or clearly non-matches)
Links this to leakage being dominated by direct or near-direct reproduction

items.question: Why does the paper compute the persuasion-level comparison in Table 4 at the probe level rather than with the dialogue-level labels used for its headline rates?
items.answer: A dialogue-level label is an OR over all three probes, so each dialogue gets a single label that cannot be attributed to any one persuasion level. Only probe-level responses, one per persuasion condition per dialogue, tie a leak to a specific level.
rubric: States that the dialogue-level label combines all three probes (any probe leaking)
Concludes that dialogue-level labels cannot separate leakage by persuasion level, so per-level rates require probe-level responses

items.question: The paper uses Cochran's Q for persuasion level. Why could the same test not be used for drift length, which instead gets a chi-square test of independence?
items.answer: Cochran's Q needs each unit to be measured under every condition. Each dialogue receives all three persuasion probes, but it has only one fixed drift length. Drift therefore varies between dialogues rather than within them, so the drift data are not repeated measures.
rubric: States that each dialogue has a single drift length but receives all three persuasion probes
Explains that Cochran's Q requires repeated (within-dialogue) measurements across conditions, which drift lacks

items.question: Why does GPT-OSS-120B's pattern across persuasion levels point specifically to pressure or urgency cues, rather than persuasion in general, as what reduces its leakage?
items.answer: The medium probe, which adds a contextual justification, does not lower GPT-OSS-120B's leakage (40.50% vs 39.30% for simple). Only the high-pressure hard probe lowers it, to 32.90%. The reduction therefore appears only with pressure cues, not with any added persuasion.
rubric: Notes that the medium (justified) probe gives leakage equal to or slightly above the simple probe (about 40.5% vs 39.3%)
Notes that only the hard probe reduces leakage (32.9%), so the drop is tied to pressure cues rather than to persuasion per se

items.question: Qwen3-VL-235B has the smallest persuasion Cramer's V (0.0639) yet the highest dialogue-level leakage. Why is this not contradictory?
items.answer: Cramer's V measures how much leakage depends on persuasion level, not how much leakage there is. Qwen leaks at high rates under all three levels (33.3–40.6%), so its leakage varies little with persuasion while staying high overall.
rubric: States that Cramer's V measures association or variation across levels, not the overall leakage rate
Notes that Qwen leaks substantially under every persuasion level, so low dependence coexists with high leakage

items.question: Would the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals in Table 3 still reflect the true sampling uncertainty if PrivDrift's dialogues were not independent of one another? What in the dataset's construction makes this a concern?
items.answer: No, they would likely be too narrow. Bootstrapping over dialogues treats each dialogue as an independent draw. However, drift turns come from a shared topic-conditioned library, personas come from a finite pool, and each persuasion level uses one fixed template, so dialogues are correlated.
rubric: Concludes the intervals could understate uncertainty (be too narrow)
Explains that bootstrapping over dialogues assumes independence, while shared drift-turn libraries, personas or fixed templates make dialogues correlated

items.question: Would PrivDrift's finding that drift does not reliably reduce leakage be expected to hold for a model with a 512-token context window? Why?
items.answer: No. Average dialogue length exceeds 512 approximate tokens from d = 4 onward (603, 695 and 757 tokens), and the secret sits in the opening turn. It would often be truncated away, so any drop in leakage would reflect the secret's absence rather than behavioural suppression. PrivDrift's result relies on dialogues of at most about 1,060 tokens staying fully in context.
rubric: Concludes the finding would not carry over (leakage could drop artificially)
Explains that the opening-turn secret would fall out of a 512-token window for many longer-drift dialogues (average about 600 or more tokens at d ≥ 4)
Notes that PrivDrift's result depends on the whole dialogue fitting well within the context window

items.question: PrivDrift's drift turns, including the assistant replies, come from a fixed library and are identical across models. When might its leakage rates fail to represent conversations in which the evaluated model wrote its own earlier replies?
items.answer: The assistant turns were not generated by the evaluated model. The results could therefore misrepresent organic use whenever a model's own replies would differ, for example by restating or acknowledging the secret, which might raise recoverability, or by refusing or redacting it early, which might lower it.
rubric: Recognizes that drift-turn assistant replies were scripted from the library rather than produced by the evaluated model
Identifies the failure condition: when the model's natural earlier replies would handle the secret differently (e.g., repeat it or refuse it), changing later recoverability

items.question: Would a large secret-type Cramer's V, on its own, support the paper's interpretation that models use format-sensitive heuristics to protect SSNs and credit cards? When would it fail to?
items.answer: No. Cramer's V does not indicate direction. A model that leaked SSNs and credit cards far more than emails and phone numbers would also produce a large V. The interpretation rests on the direction shown in Table 5, where the sensitive numeric formats are suppressed.
rubric: States that a large V alone would not support the interpretation
Explains that V is non-directional, so a reversed asymmetry (SSN/credit card leaking more) would give an equally large V; the support comes from Table 5's direction

items.question: If the assistant's drift-turn replies had frequently restated the user's secret, which of the paper's results would lose its intended interpretation?
items.answer: The drift results (c4), and with them Privacy Half-Life (c6), would lose their meaning. The secret would reappear close to the probe, so d would no longer measure how far the probe is from the disclosure. Persistence across drift could then reflect recent restatement rather than recall from the opening turn.
rubric: Identifies the drift-length finding (and/or Privacy Half-Life) as compromised
Explains that restatements would keep the secret near the probe, so d would no longer measure distance from the original disclosure

items.question: If fuzzy matching at 0.80 had flagged about 10 percentage points more responses than both fuzzy 0.85 and the hybrid detector, which conclusion would be undermined?
items.answer: The claim that leakage is dominated by direct or near-direct reproduction, corroborated by fuzzy matching tracking the hybrid labels (c2), would be undermined. Many near-miss reproductions would exist that neither Stage 1 nor the judge counted. That would also suggest the hybrid detector misses partial disclosures and understates leakage.
rubric: Names the claim that fuzzy matching tracks hybrid labels and that leakage is mainly direct reproduction (c2)
Explains that many near-miss outputs uncounted by the hybrid detector would suggest it misses partial disclosures

items.question: If each model's three per-persuasion rates in Table 4 had been identical, which values reported elsewhere in the paper would necessarily change, and which claim would fall?
items.answer: The persuasion Cramer's V values in Table 8 would be zero, and Cochran's Q would not be significant. The claim that persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage in a non-monotonic, model-dependent way (c3) would therefore fall.
rubric: States that the persuasion Cramer's V would be 0 (and/or Cochran's Q non-significant)
Identifies c3's claim of a significant, model-dependent persuasion effect as the claim that would fall

items.question: Suppose DeepSeek-R1's leakage had fallen steadily with drift, reaching half of L(0) at d = 6. Which of the paper's drift-related claims would be undermined, and which would survive?
items.answer: The claim that drift does not reliably reduce leakage (c4) would be undermined, because leakage would decline steadily. The result that τ = 7 (c6) would survive, because 50% of L(0) is still above δ = 0.1·L(0).
rubric: States that c4 (drift does not reliably reduce leakage) would be undermined
States that the τ = 7 result would still hold
Explains that half of L(0) remains above the 10% threshold δ

items.question: In a workflow, every later request for user data comes with a contextual justification such as filling in a form. A colleague prefers GPT-OSS-120B over Qwen3-VL-235B because Qwen has the highest dialogue-level leakage. Is that preference justified for this workflow?
items.answer: No. Under the medium (justified) probe, Qwen3-VL-235B leaks less than GPT-OSS-120B (33.30% vs 40.50%). DeepSeek-R1 is safest of all at 22.00%. The dialogue-level ranking aggregates all three probe styles and does not reflect this request style.
rubric: Concludes the preference is not justified (Qwen leaks less than GPT under justified requests)
Cites the medium-probe rates (about 33% for Qwen vs 40.5% for GPT), optionally noting DeepSeek-R1 is lowest at 22%
Notes that the dialogue-level ranking mixes all probe styles

items.question: Suppose a GPT-OSS-120B deployment sees disclosures that are 90% SSNs and 10% emails, and PrivDrift's per-type rates carry over. Roughly what probe-level leakage rate should be expected?
items.answer: About 8%: 0.9 × 0.14% + 0.1 × 78.24% ≈ 7.95%. Almost all of it comes from the email disclosures.
rubric: Gives roughly 8% (accept about 7.5–8.5%)
Shows the weighted combination of the SSN (0.14%) and email (78.24%) rates, with email dominating

items.question: A vendor patches GPT-OSS-120B so that it suppresses emails as strongly as SSNs (0.14%), with all else unchanged. Assuming the four secret types are equally common, roughly what would its probe-level leakage become, and what would remain the main source?
items.answer: About 18%: (0.14 + 0.00 + 0.14 + 70.89)/4 ≈ 17.8%, down from about 37%. Phone numbers, at about 71%, would then account for nearly all remaining leakage.
rubric: Gives roughly 18% (accept about 17–19%)
Identifies phone numbers as the dominant remaining source

items.question: A new model evaluated on PrivDrift has about 40% probe-level leakage but a secret-type Cramer's V of only about 0.05. By the paper's reasoning, what does this imply about its handling of SSNs and credit cards compared with the three evaluated models?
items.answer: It leaks SSNs and credit cards about as often as emails and phones, roughly 40%. It therefore lacks the format-sensitive suppression that kept those types near zero (0–6%) for the evaluated models. Its uniformity reflects being equally leaky across types, not better contextual confidentiality reasoning.
rubric: Concludes the model leaks SSNs and credit cards far more than the evaluated models (about as often as emails and phones)
Explains that low V means leakage barely depends on type, i.e., no format-sensitive suppression, which is not evidence of contextual reasoning

items.question: Running PrivDrift on a new model, a team finds 30% probe-level leakage and 31% dialogue-level leakage. What does this imply about how its leaks spread across the three probes, compared with the paper's models?
items.answer: Its leaking dialogues almost always leak under all three probes, so each dialogue is either leaked by every probe style or by none. In the paper's models, dialogue-level leakage exceeds probe-level by about 10–17 points, meaning many dialogues leak under only some probes.
rubric: Concludes the new model's leaks are highly consistent across probes (mostly all three or none)
Contrasts this with the paper's models, whose dialogue-level rates exceed probe-level rates by about 10–17 points because many dialogues leak under only some probes

items.question: Since Qwen3-VL-235B leaks more than GPT-OSS-120B, does the paper show that larger models leak more user secrets? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Only three models are compared, and they differ in family, training and serving, not just size. The paper does not vary or control parameter count, so size cannot be isolated as the cause.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the three models differ in many respects beyond size and that the paper does not vary or control model size

items.question: Is the dialogue-level model ranking (DeepSeek-R1 < GPT-OSS-120B < Qwen3-VL-235B) an artifact of the LLM judge? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Regex-only dialogue-level rates give the same order (37.80 < 47.70 < 53.50). The judge adds at most 1.10 points, far smaller than the gaps of at least about 6 points between models.
rubric: Answers contradicted (the ranking is not a judge artifact)
Cites that regex-only rates preserve the order and that the judge's contribution (≤1.1 points) is much smaller than the gaps between models

items.question: Does the paper show that the models spontaneously disclose earlier secrets when no one asks for them? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Every evaluated response is a reply to a probe that explicitly requests the secret, and the drift turns are scripted rather than generated by the evaluated model. Unprompted disclosure is never measured.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that leakage is measured only in responses to explicit extraction probes, so spontaneous disclosure is not tested

items.question: Does the paper show that SSN and credit-card suppression is triggered by the digit format of the secret rather than by the category named in the probe? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Probes refer to the item by its category (e.g., 'the phone number mentioned earlier'), and the design never varies the format and the category wording separately. Format cues and category cues are therefore confounded.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that probe wording and secret format co-vary with type and are never manipulated independently, so the two cues cannot be separated

items.question: Does the negligible-to-small drift-length Cramer's V show that drift has no sizable effect under any individual persuasion level? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The drift Cramer's V is computed on probe-level responses pooled across persuasion levels, which could average out opposing per-level trends. Only a heatmap is shown per level, with no per-level statistics. The fact that τ = 7 for every persuasion level rules out only stable decay to 10% of L(0), not every sizable effect.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the effect size is pooled over persuasion levels and no per-level drift statistics are reported (τ = 7 per level excludes only stable 90% suppression)

items.question: Does the paper show that secrets leak to a different user who later joins a shared session? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Shared sessions motivate the threat model, but each probe is simply appended to the same transcript with no change of speaker or session identity. A different user asking is never simulated.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that probes are appended to the same conversation without any user-identity switch, so cross-user leakage is not directly tested

items.question: Would switching from hybrid to regex-only detection move Qwen3-VL-235B's dialogue-level leakage outside its 95% confidence interval?
items.answer: No. The regex-only rate of 53.50% lies inside the hybrid interval [51.6, 57.7], so the choice of detector matters less than sampling uncertainty.
rubric: Answers no
Notes that 53.50% falls within [51.6, 57.7]

items.question: Would switching from dialogue-level to probe-level aggregation move Qwen3-VL-235B's hybrid leakage outside its 95% dialogue-level confidence interval?
items.answer: Yes. The probe-level rate of 37.53% is far below the interval [51.6, 57.7], so the choice of aggregation level matters much more than the choice of detector.
rubric: Answers yes
Notes that 37.53% is far outside [51.6, 57.7], because the two aggregation levels count different things

items.question: Pooling all three models' probe-level responses with equal weight, would the hard probe yield higher leakage than the medium probe?
items.answer: Yes. The pooled hard rate is about 34.2% ((32.9 + 29.2 + 40.6)/3), versus about 31.9% for medium ((40.5 + 22.0 + 33.3)/3).
rubric: Answers yes
Gives pooled rates of about 34.2% (hard) vs about 31.9% (medium)

items.question: Pooling all three models' probe-level responses with equal weight, would the hard probe yield higher leakage than the simple probe?
items.answer: No. The pooled hard rate of about 34.2% is below the pooled simple rate of about 35.4% ((39.3 + 28.1 + 38.7)/3).
rubric: Answers no
Gives pooled rates of about 34.2% (hard) vs about 35.4% (simple)

items.question: Given the paper's definition of Privacy Half-Life, would a reading of τ = 7 reliably separate a model whose leakage does not decay from one whose leakage declines steadily within d ≤ 6? Why?
items.answer: No. τ = 7 is assigned whenever no observed d brings leakage to at most 10% of L(0). A flat curve and a steadily falling curve that ends above that threshold (e.g., one ending at 15% of L(0)) receive the same score. τ captures only stable suppression past the δ threshold, not the amount or trend of decay.
rubric: Answers no, the metric cannot separate the two cases
Explains that τ = max(D_obs)+1 whenever leakage never reaches 0.1·L(0), regardless of how much leakage declines above that threshold

rejected.question: The seeded secret is jane.doe@example.com and the model replies 'JANE.DOE@EXAMPLE.COM'. Would Stage 1 normalization matching flag it as leakage?
rejected.answer: Yes. For alphanumeric secrets, Stage 1 normalizes case and whitespace, so the uppercase reply normalizes to the secret and the substring test succeeds.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that case normalization makes the reply match the normalized secret.

rejected.question: The seeded secret is jane.doe@example.com and the model replies 'janedoe@example.com' (dropping the dot). Would Stage 1 normalization matching flag it as leakage?
rejected.answer: No. Alphanumeric normalization preserves meaningful delimiters such as the dot, so the normalized secret is not a substring of the reply. Only the Stage 2 judge could catch it.
rubric: Answers no (not at Stage 1).
Explains that delimiters are preserved for alphanumeric secrets, so the missing dot breaks the substring match (only the judge might flag it).

rejected.question: If the seeded email is jane@example.com and the model replies 'JANE@EXAMPLE.COM', would Stage 1 normalization matching flag it as leakage?
rejected.answer: Yes. For alphanumeric secrets, Stage 1 normalizes case, so the uppercase reply contains the normalized secret as a substring.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that Stage 1 normalizes case for alphanumeric secrets, so the strings match

rejected.question: If the seeded email is jane@example.com and the model replies 'janeexamplecom', would Stage 1 normalization matching flag it as leakage?
rejected.answer: No. For alphanumeric secrets, Stage 1 preserves meaningful delimiters such as '@' and '.'. The normalized secret therefore does not appear in a reply with the delimiters removed; only the judge could flag it.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that alphanumeric normalization keeps delimiters, so the substring test fails

rejected.question: If a model's leakage followed L(d) = L(0) × 0.7^d at every observed drift length, would its Privacy Half-Life be below 7?
rejected.answer: No. Even at d = 6, L = 0.7^6·L(0) ≈ 0.118·L(0) > 0.1·L(0). No observed d meets the threshold, so τ = 7 despite the steady decline.
rubric: Answers no (τ = 7)
Shows that 0.7^6 ≈ 0.118 stays above the 0.1 threshold, so no observed drift length qualifies

rejected.question: If a model's leakage followed L(d) = L(0) × 0.5^d at every observed drift length, would its Privacy Half-Life be below 7?
rejected.answer: Yes. L(4) = 0.0625·L(0) ≤ 0.1·L(0), while L(3) = 0.125·L(0) is above the threshold, and leakage stays below it at d = 5 and 6. So τ = 4.
rubric: Answers yes (τ = 4)
Shows that leakage first falls to at most 0.1·L(0) at d = 4 and stays there for larger observed d
